claims.text: The starting coating has a dual-phase FCC/BCC microstructure with coherent, well-defined interphase boundaries.
Sustained mechanical loading at constant stress causes progressive plastic deformation in the coating.
At moderate temperature, dislocation glide and limited diffusion dominate deformation.
Coherent FCC/BCC interphase boundaries promote local dislocation pile-up.
Coherent FCC/BCC boundaries hinder dislocation transmission between neighboring regions.
Dislocations generated in FCC, and possibly BCC, regions accumulate at coherent FCC/BCC boundaries during loading.
Dislocation pile-ups at interfaces generate local back-stresses.
The resulting local stress fields restrain further dislocation motion.
Restricting dislocation motion delays creep-related plastic flow.
A randomized or less coherent FCC/BCC phase arrangement lacks the same effective dislocation barrier.
A coating with reduced interfacial coherence will exhibit higher creep strain than a coherent-interface coating under identical conditions.
The coherent-interface coating will have lower incremental creep strain or creep strain rate than the disrupted-interface baseline.
The coherent-interface coating will have a longer creep lifetime than the disrupted-interface baseline.
Pronounced dislocation pile-ups will be observed at FCC/BCC interfaces in the high-coherence sample.
The proposed mechanism dominates only before diffusion-driven creep or stress-induced phase transformations become predominant.
Increasing stress and temperature accelerates creep by enhancing diffusion and activating deformation carriers.
Grain orientation can affect dislocation pile-up and the effectiveness of an interface as a barrier.
A modified thermal cycle can selectively reduce FCC/BCC interfacial coherence and produce a randomized phase distribution while enabling an otherwise controlled comparison.

contradictions.description: The two sets are described as having nominally identical processing histories, but they are then assigned different post-processing or thermal cycles. The interface treatment is necessarily a processing-history difference and may introduce confounding microstructural changes.
